props.title: The Last Shepherd

sections.content: **The Last Shepherd** (2013) represents a vital entry in contemporary documentary filmmaking about vanishing traditional ways of life, following in the footsteps of works like Le Quattro Volte (2010) and Sweetgrass (2009). Director Marco Bonfanti crafts an intimate portrait of Renato Zucchelli, Milan's last traveling shepherd, whose determination to keep ancient pastoral traditions alive amid urban sprawl creates striking visual contrasts. The film's power comes from juxtaposing sheep moving through concrete landscapes, much like the memorable sequences in **Faces Places** (2017) where Agnès Varda explores rural French traditions colliding with modernity.

sections.content: The documentary tradition of capturing disappearing rural lifestyles gained particular momentum in the 2010s, with films like **The Shepherd** (2016) and **Stray Dogs** (2013) examining how urbanization impacts traditional professions. Bonfanti's approach stands out for its warmth and whimsy, allowing moments of joy to punctuate the underlying melancholy of watching a centuries-old way of life fade away. The director's choice to include children's perspectives creates an additional layer of poignancy, reminiscent of **The Eagle Huntress** (2016). SUBHEAD: Urban-Rural Divide in Contemporary Documentary

What elevates **The Last Shepherd** beyond simple pastoral nostalgia is its nuanced exploration of how traditional practices might survive in modern contexts. Like **Honeyland** (2019) and **The Biggest Little Farm** (2018), the film suggests that ancient wisdom and contemporary life aren't necessarily incompatible. Zucchelli's mission to bring his sheep to Milan's children becomes a powerful metaphor for bridging urban-rural divides, similar to themes explored in **Gunda** (2020) and **Time of the Gypsies** (1988).
